label: Chapter 2
name: Time Value of Money: Simple and Compound Interest

questions.q: How do banks make a profit margin on interest?
o: By paying lower interest on deposits than they charge on loans
By paying higher interest on deposits than on loans
By charging interest only on deposits
By lending only their own money
questions.d: Interest rate margin: banks pay lower interest on deposits and charge higher interest on loans.
questions.w: The difference between the two rates is the bank's profit margin. In Oman, deposit rates are about 0.5% to 5% p.a. and lending rates about 1.50% to 7% p.a.

questions.q: According to the notes, deposit interest rates in Oman range from about:
questions.d: Interest rates in Oman: deposit rates 0.5% to 5% p.a.; lending rates 1.50% to 7% p.a., depending on the product.
questions.w: 1.50% to 7% is the lending range. Deposit rates are lower, which creates the bank's margin.

questions.q: Simple interest is calculated on:
o: The principal plus interest from previous periods
questions.d: Simple interest: interest calculated only on the principal deposited or borrowed. I = P × r × t.
questions.w: Interest on accumulated interest is compound interest. Simple interest always uses the original principal.

questions.q: How much interest does RO 1,000 earn at 4% simple interest for 15 months?
questions.d: Simple interest: I = P × r × t, where t must be in years.
questions.w: 15 months = 15 ÷ 12 = 1.25 years. I = 1,000 × 0.04 × 1.25 = RO 50. Using 15 as years would give RO 600, which is wrong.

questions.q: A deposit of RO 4,000 earned RO 360 simple interest in 3 years. What is the rate?
questions.d: Rate from simple interest: r = I ÷ (P × t).

questions.q: What principal earns RO 250 simple interest in 5 years at 5%?
questions.d: Principal from simple interest: P = I ÷ (r × t).

questions.q: How long must RO 2,500 be deposited at 4% simple interest to earn RO 500?
questions.d: Time from simple interest: t = I ÷ (P × r).
questions.w: t = 500 ÷ (2,500 × 0.04) = 500 ÷ 100 = 5 years. (For RO 5,000 at 5% it would be 2 years.)

questions.q: If interest is compounded quarterly, the compounding factor n is:
questions.d: Compounding factor n: annually 1, semi-annually 2, quarterly 4, monthly 12, daily 365 or 366.
questions.w: There are four quarters in a year, so interest is added 4 times.

questions.q: Which formula gives the compound INTEREST (not the final amount)?
questions.d: Compound interest: I = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) − P.
questions.w: P(1 + r/n)^(nt) is the total amount (future value). Subtracting P leaves only the interest. P × r × t is simple interest.

questions.q: How much interest does RO 500 earn at 12% for 2 years, compounded annually?
questions.d: Compound interest: I = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) − P.
questions.w: I = 500 × (1 + 0.12)^2 − 500 = 500 × 1.2544 − 500 = RO 127.200. RO 120 is simple interest; RO 627.200 is the total amount.

questions.q: RO 500 is invested at 12% for 2 years. Which compounding frequency earns the MOST interest?
questions.d: More frequent compounding means interest is added and starts earning interest sooner.
questions.w: Annually RO 127.200, semi-annually RO 131.238, quarterly RO 133.385, monthly RO 134.867. Monthly is highest.

questions.q: For a 5-year deposit, which is better: 12% compounded monthly or 12.5% compounded annually?
questions.d: Compare schemes by their growth factor (1 + r/n)^(nt) over the same period.
questions.w: 12% monthly: (1.01)^60 = 1.8167. 12.5% annually: (1.125)^5 = 1.8020. The monthly scheme grows more, whatever the principal.

questions.q: For a 4-year deposit, which is better: 5% compounded monthly or 5.25% simple interest?
questions.d: Simple interest grows by r × t; compound interest grows by (1 + r/n)^(nt) − 1.
questions.w: Compound: (1 + 0.05/12)^48 − 1 = 22.09% total. Simple: 5.25% × 4 = 21% total. Compound gives more.

questions.q: RO 420 interest was earned in 2 years at 10% compounded annually. What was the principal?
questions.d: Principal from compound interest: P = I ÷ [(1 + r/n)^(nt) − 1].

questions.q: Ali borrows RO 1,000 for 4 years at 5% simple interest and invests it at 6% compounded quarterly for 4 years. What is his net benefit?
questions.d: Benefit = interest earned on the investment − interest paid on the loan.

questions.q: Sameer deposits RO 2,000 at 10% compounded quarterly. How much does he receive after 9 months?
questions.d: Future amount: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt).
questions.w: 9 months = 0.75 years, so nt = 4 × 0.75 = 3 quarters. A = 2,000 × (1.025)^3 = RO 2,153.781, so interest = RO 153.781.

questions.q: Using the Rule of 72, how long does money take to double at 9% per annum?
questions.d: Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ interest rate (compounded annually).
questions.w: 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years.

questions.q: You want your investment to double in 6 years. Using the Rule of 72, what rate do you need?
questions.d: Rule of 72 rearranged: rate ≈ 72 ÷ years to double.

questions.q: At 12% for 18 years, how many times will an investment DOUBLE, using the Rule of 72?
questions.d: Rule of 72: doubling time = 72 ÷ rate. Number of doublings = total years ÷ doubling time.
questions.w: Doubling time = 72 ÷ 12 = 6 years. 18 ÷ 6 = 3 doublings, so the money grows 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times its original value.

questions.q: The Rule of 72 has a high estimation error when:
o: Interest rates are very low or very high
The investment is in a bank
questions.d: Rule of 72: a quick estimate of doubling time, assuming annual compounding.
questions.w: It is only an approximation. The notes warn the error is high at very low or very high interest rates.

questions.q: How do you calculate simple interest in Excel?
o: Type a formula such as =Principal*Rate*Time; there is no built-in function
questions.d: Excel has no built-in simple interest function; you build the equation yourself.
questions.w: The slides say to calculate interest using =Principal*Rate*Time and press Enter.

questions.q: At the same rate, it is better to borrow at simple interest and invest at compound interest.
questions.d: Over the same period and rate, compound interest is higher than simple interest after the first year.
questions.w: Borrowing at simple interest means paying less; investing at compound interest means earning more.

questions.q: For daily compounding, n = 52.
questions.d: Compounding factor for daily compounding: n = 365 or 366.
questions.w: 52 is the number of weeks in a year, not days.

questions.q: At 7%, RO 1,000 earns RO 140 simple interest and RO 144.90 compound interest (annual) over 2 years.
questions.d: Simple: P × r × t. Compound: P(1 + r)^t − P.

questions.q: Under compound interest, interest is also earned on the interest added in previous periods.
questions.d: Compound interest: interest is calculated on the outstanding principal and on the interest accumulated from previous periods.
questions.w: That is exactly what 'compounding' means.

questions.q: You deposit RO 5,000 in Bank Muscat at 5% simple interest and RO 2,500 in Bank Ahli at 4% simple interest. For each, how long will it take to earn RO 500 interest?
questions.d: Simple interest: I = P × r × t, so t = I ÷ (P × r).
questions.w: Bank Muscat reaches the target faster because both its principal and rate are higher, so it earns RO 250 a year against Bank Ahli's RO 100.

questions.q: A bank offers a 5-year fixed deposit at (I) 12% compounded monthly or (II) 12.5% compounded annually. Which is better? Show the working for a deposit of RO 1,000.
questions.d: Future amount with compound interest: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt).
questions.w: Even with a lower stated rate, monthly compounding adds interest 60 times, and each addition earns interest. That beats one annual addition at 12.5%.

questions.q: Ali borrowed RO 1,000 for 4 years at 5% simple interest and invested it at 6% compounded quarterly for 4 years. How much does he benefit?
questions.a:
Interest paid on loan = 1,000 × 0.05 × 4 = RO 200.000
Amount from investment = 1,000 × (1 + 0.06/4)^(4×4) = 1,000 × (1.015)^16 = RO 1,268.986
Interest earned = RO 268.986
Benefit = RO 268.986 − 200.000 = RO 68.986
questions.d: Benefit = interest earned − interest paid.
questions.w: He gains because he pays simple interest at 5% but earns compound interest at 6%.

questions.q: Zubin invested some money at 4% p.a. simple interest for 3 years and received RO 11,200 in total. He kept the interest aside and invested the same principal at 10% compound interest (annual) for 4 more years. Find the amount from the second investment and the total interest from both.
questions.a:
First investment: A = P(1 + rt) → 11,200 = P × (1 + 0.04 × 3) = P × 1.12 → P = RO 10,000
Interest from first = 11,200 − 10,000 = RO 1,200
Second investment: A = 10,000 × (1.10)^4 = RO 14,641.000
Interest from second = RO 4,641.000
Total interest = 1,200 + 4,641 = RO 5,841.000
questions.d: Simple interest amount: A = P(1 + rt). Compound amount: A = P(1 + r)^t.
questions.w: Find the principal first from the simple interest total, then grow the same principal with compound interest.

questions.q: Find the interest on RO 20,000 invested for 4 years at 12% compounded (a) annually, (b) semi-annually, (c) quarterly, (d) monthly.
questions.d: Compound interest: I = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) − P.
questions.w: The more often interest is compounded, the higher the interest, because each addition starts earning interest sooner.

questions.q: Rafael is 22 and invests RO 2,000 in Oman development bonds at 7.5%. Using the Rule of 72, how many times will his money double by age 70, and what will it grow to?
questions.a:
Years invested = 70 − 22 = 48 years
Doubling time = 72 ÷ 7.5 = 9.6 years
Number of doublings = 48 ÷ 9.6 = 5
Value = 2,000 × 2^5 = 2,000 × 32 = RO 64,000
questions.d: Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate.
questions.w: Each doubling multiplies the money by 2, so 5 doublings multiply it by 32.
